knowledge_meta.name: Universal Discovery Framework
knowledge_meta.description: Industry-agnostic question frameworks, perspective definitions, and cross-perspective connection rules. This pack is always loaded alongside an industry-specific pack.

financial.name: Financial
financial.purpose: Account for and report financial position
financial.discovery_description: Start with the business questions leadership asks, then trace backwards to the data needed to answer them. Financial discovery defines the DEMAND — what data is needed and why.
financial.key_principle: Every metric must answer a business question. If nobody asks the question, the metric doesn't matter.

management.name: Management
management.discovery_description: Connect upward to financial metrics and downward to operational data. Management is the MEASUREMENT FUNCTION — it translates operational reality into performance indicators that feed financial decisions.
management.key_principle: Management is not a layer — it's a perspective. Every operational area has a management view. The question is: how do we measure if this area is performing well?

operational.name: Operational
operational.discovery_description: Map what actually happens on the ground — who does what, using which systems, creating what data. Operational discovery reveals the SUPPLY — what data actually exists and where it's born.
operational.key_principle: Data is born at the point of activity. The closer to the activity, the more reliable the data. Every step away introduces delay, interpretation, and potential error.

phases.name: Business Questions
phases.description: Identify the top questions leadership asks about financial performance

questions.text: What are the top 3 financial questions your leadership team asks each period?
follow_ups: How quickly do you need those answers?
Who asks these questions and in what context (board meeting, monthly review, ad-hoc)?
hints: Common: revenue vs target, cost variance, profitability by segment, cash position
The frequency of asking reveals urgency — daily questions need real-time data, quarterly questions can tolerate month-end cycles

questions.text: What decisions depend on these financial answers? What happens differently if the answer is good vs bad?
follow_ups: How quickly does a decision need to be made once the data is available?
hints: Connect metrics to decisions: 'If margin drops below X, we do Y' — this validates the metric matters
If no decision changes based on the answer, the metric may not be worth tracking

phases.name: Metric Definition
phases.description: Define metrics precisely — what exactly is being measured and how

questions.text: For each question, let's define exactly what we're measuring. What does 'good' look like — what's the target or benchmark?
follow_ups: Is this measured at the total level, or broken down by segment/project/product?
hints: A metric without a target is just a number. Targets create context for interpretation
Segmentation reveals where the insight lives — overall margin may look fine but one segment could be losing money

phases.name: Measure Tracing
phases.description: Trace each metric to the calculations that produce it

questions.text: How do you calculate this metric today? Walk me through the formula — what numbers go in?
follow_ups: Where does each number come from?
Are there any adjustments or manual steps in the calculation?
hints: Metrics → Measures → Attributes is the tracing chain
Manual adjustments often hide important business logic that should be documented
If the formula is 'it's in an Excel formula somewhere', that's a shadow system

phases.name: Data Sourcing
phases.description: Identify where the raw data lives and how reliable it is

questions.text: For each data point, which system is the source of truth? Is that the same system where people actually maintain the data?
follow_ups: How fresh is this data — real-time, daily, weekly, monthly?
What happens when the data is wrong — who notices and how is it corrected?
hints: Source of truth ≠ where data is used. The gap between them is where data quality breaks
Freshness determines how current your metrics can be — you can't have real-time KPIs from monthly data

phases.name: Monitoring & KPIs
phases.description: Understand what managers monitor and how they know things are on track

questions.text: What do you check first thing to know if things are running smoothly? What signals trouble?
follow_ups: How do you currently get this information?
What's the gap between 'problem happens' and 'you know about it'?
hints: The monitoring question reveals what managers actually care about vs what they're told to care about
Early warning indicators are more valuable than lagging indicators — but harder to define

phases.name: Connect Up to Financial
phases.description: Link management KPIs to the financial outcomes they influence

questions.text: Which of your KPIs have a direct financial impact? If this KPI degrades, what happens to the bottom line?
follow_ups: Can you quantify the financial impact?
Are there leading indicators that predict financial problems before they show up?
hints: This connection is the value chain: operational excellence → management KPIs → financial outcomes
Leading indicators (e.g., declining velocity) predict lagging outcomes (e.g., budget overrun)

phases.name: Connect Down to Operational
phases.description: Link management monitoring to the operational data it depends on

questions.text: What data do you need from the people doing the work? What do you chase them for?
follow_ups: How reliable is the data you receive?
What's the lag between activity and your visibility of it?
hints: The 'chase' question reveals data gaps — things managers need but can't easily get
Reliability and freshness are the two dimensions of data quality from a management perspective

phases.name: Pain Points
phases.description: Identify management pain points and workarounds

questions.text: What's the most time-consuming part of your management role that feels like it should be easier?
follow_ups: How many hours per week does this take?
Are there Excel spreadsheets you couldn't function without?
hints: Pain points reveal process improvement opportunities
Shadow spreadsheets reveal gaps in system capability

phases.name: Systems & People
phases.description: Map the systems and roles involved in daily operations

questions.text: Walk me through a typical day. What systems do people touch, and in what order?
follow_ups: Which systems are essential vs optional?
How many tool switches happen in a single workflow?
hints: Tool switches = potential data breaks. 3+ switches in one workflow = high waste
Systems people skip reveal data gaps downstream

phases.name: Data Creation
phases.description: Understand where and how data is born at the point of activity

questions.text: When work gets done, how is it recorded? Is the recording automatic or manual?
follow_ups: How quickly is it recorded — real-time, same day, end of week?
What happens if recording is delayed or missed?
hints: Automatic recording = high reliability. Manual = variable. Batch entry = low granularity
The gap between 'work done' and 'work recorded' is the freshness risk

phases.name: Entities & Relationships
phases.description: Identify core business objects and their relationships

questions.text: What are the main 'things' you work with — orders, products, customers, projects, tickets? How do they relate?
follow_ups: Is there a hierarchy — e.g., customer → order → line item?
Do the same things mean different things to different teams?
hints: Entity identification is the foundation. Get the nouns right first, then the relationships
If the same entity means different things to different teams — that's a lens, not a new entity

phases.name: Pain Points & Workarounds
phases.description: Identify operational friction, manual effort, and shadow systems

questions.text: What's the most annoying admin task that takes you away from your real work?
follow_ups: How much time per week does this take?
If you could fix one data problem, what would it be?
hints: Admin friction × people × frequency = total waste hours/month
The 'magic wand' question reveals the highest-impact opportunity

cross_perspective_connections.description: Financial costs originate from operational data capture. Tracing costs back to their source reveals data quality risks.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Where does this cost data originate? Who enters it and in which system?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Financial reports depend on management-curated data like approvals, status updates, and forecasts.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: What management processes feed this financial report? Is there a handoff or approval step?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Management data quality issues often stem from operational data capture gaps.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Why is this data unreliable — is it a capture problem at the operational level?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Management insights need financial context to drive decisions.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: What's the financial impact of this KPI? Can we quantify the cost of poor performance here?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Operational data that nobody monitors suggests missing management metrics.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Is anyone monitoring this data at a management level? Should they be?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Operational activities directly drive financial transactions.
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How does this operational activity translate into a financial entry? What's the chain?

waste_categories.description: Standard waste categories for process step classification

categories.name: Manual Data Entry
categories.description: Information that could be captured automatically but requires human typing
indicators: Re-keying data from one system to another
Copying values from email/chat into a system

categories.name: System Switching
categories.description: Tasks that require switching between multiple systems to complete
indicators: Looking up information in one tool to enter in another

categories.name: Manual Verification
categories.description: Checking that data is correct when it could be validated automatically
indicators: Reviewing data that came from another system

categories.name: Waiting Time
categories.description: Delays caused by approvals, system processing, or data availability

categories.name: Physical Media
categories.description: Paper, printed reports, or physical artifacts that could be digital

crystallisation_guide.description: Framework for identifying when data crystallises — becomes a frozen, trusted fact
key_questions: At what point does this data become 'official' — i.e., decisions are made based on it?
Is there an approval step that locks the data?
Can the data be changed after it's been used for reporting?
What process step makes this data go from 'draft/tentative' to 'final/committed'?

common_crystallisation_points.example: Timesheet approval crystallises hours for billing
GL posting crystallises revenue and cost entries
SOW signing crystallises scope, budget, and timeline
Inventory cutoff crystallises stock quantities for valuation
